questions.question: What is JUnit 5 and how do you write a basic test?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Basics Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **JUnit 5 is the standard Java unit testing framework.** A basic test is a method annotated with `@Test`. Assert results with `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, etc. JUnit 5 consists of three modules: JUnit Platform, JUnit Jupiter (the API), and JUnit Vintage (backward compatibility).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical JUnit knowledge — can you write a test right now?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using JUnit 4 import (org.junit.Test) in a JUnit 5 project — annotations look the same but packages differ
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the three modules of JUnit 5 and that @Test comes from org.junit.jupiter.api

sections.title: JUnit 5 Architecture
sections.content: JUnit 5 = **JUnit Platform** (test engine runner) + **JUnit Jupiter** (new API, `@Test` annotations) + **JUnit Vintage** (runs JUnit 3/4 tests). Import: `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test`. Basic test structure: class with no special parent, methods annotated `@Test`, use `Assertions.assertEquals(expected, actual)`. Tests run in IDE (right-click) or via `mvn test`. No `public` required on test methods in JUnit 5 (unlike JUnit 4).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Import: import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
- @Test annotation marks test methods
- No return value, no parameters for basic @Test
- Test class does not need to extend anything
- Methods don't need to be public (package-private is fine)
- Run with: mvn test, gradle test, or IDE run
- Maven dependency: junit-jupiter (JUnit 5 BOM)
- JUnit 4 vs 5: different package (org.junit vs org.junit.jupiter.api)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JUnit 5 is the standard Java testing framework and consists of three modules — Platform, Jupiter, and Vintage. The API I use daily is JUnit Jupiter. A basic test is just a method annotated with @Test from org.junit.jupiter.api. The test class doesn't need to extend anything. Inside the method I arrange my test data, call the method under test, and use Assertions.assertEquals to verify the result. In JUnit 5 unlike JUnit 4, test methods don't need to be public. I run tests via Maven with mvn test or through the IDE. I'd add this as a dependency in pom.xml with the junit-jupiter artifact.

questions.question: What are the most important JUnit 5 annotations?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Annotations | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Core annotations: @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll, @DisplayName, @Disabled.** @BeforeEach runs before every test (setup), @AfterEach cleans up after each test. @BeforeAll/@AfterAll run once for the class (must be static).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @BeforeEach (per test) with @BeforeAll (once per class) — and forgetting @BeforeAll must be static
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why @BeforeAll must be static: JUnit 5 creates a new instance per test by default, so a static method is the only way to run something once

sections.title: Lifecycle Annotations
sections.content: @BeforeEach: runs before each @Test method — use for common setup (new object, reset state). @AfterEach: runs after each @Test — use for cleanup (close resources). @BeforeAll: runs **once** before all tests in the class — must be `static` (since JUnit creates a new instance per test). @AfterAll: once after all tests — also static. @DisplayName: human-readable test name in reports. @Disabled: skips a test with an optional reason.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @BeforeEach: setup per test — new instance of the class under test
- @AfterEach: cleanup per test — close streams, reset mocks
- @BeforeAll: static, runs once — expensive setup (DB connection)
- @AfterAll: static, runs once — teardown
- @DisplayName: readable names for test reports
- @Disabled("reason"): skip test — marks it clearly rather than commenting out
- @Tag: categorize tests for selective running
- @Nested: inner class for grouping related tests

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The lifecycle annotations I use most are @BeforeEach and @AfterEach. @BeforeEach runs before each test method — I use it to create fresh instances of the class under test so tests don't share state. @AfterEach runs after each test for cleanup. @BeforeAll runs once before all tests in the class and must be static — that's because JUnit 5 creates a new test class instance for each test by default, so only a static context survives across all tests. I use @Disabled with a comment instead of commenting out tests — it's clearer and still shows up in reports as skipped. @DisplayName lets me write readable English descriptions for test reports.

followup_questions: Why must @BeforeAll be static in JUnit 5?
What is @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)?
How do you group tests with @Nested?

questions.question: How do you use assertions in JUnit 5?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Assertions | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **JUnit 5 assertions are in `org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions`.** Key ones: `assertEquals(expected, actual)`, `assertTrue/assertFalse`, `assertNull/assertNotNull`, `assertThrows` (for exceptions), `assertAll` (group multiple assertions). Arguments order: expected first, then actual.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical assertion knowledge — can you verify behavior correctly?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reversing expected and actual in assertEquals — the error message will say 'expected 5 but got hello' which is confusing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show assertThrows usage for exception testing and explain assertAll for grouping assertions

sections.title: Common Assertions
sections.content: `assertEquals(expected, actual)` — expected first! `assertTrue(condition)` / `assertFalse(condition)`. `assertNull(obj)` / `assertNotNull(obj)`. `assertThrows(ExceptionClass.class, () -> method())` — returns the exception for further assertions. `assertAll("group", () -> assertEquals(...), () -> assertTrue(...))` — runs all assertions even if one fails. Optional last parameter: failure message as Supplier<String> for lazy evaluation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- assertEquals(EXPECTED, actual) — convention: expected first
- assertThrows: returns exception — check message, type, etc.
- assertAll: all assertions run even if one fails — better diagnosis
- assertArrayEquals: deep equality for arrays
- assertSame/assertNotSame: reference equality (==)
- Import: import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;
- Add message param for better failure output: assertEquals(5, result, 'Tax should be 5%')
- assertDoesNotThrow: verify no exception is thrown

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JUnit 5 assertions are in the Assertions class. The most common is assertEquals where the convention is expected value first and actual value second — this matters because the error message will say 'expected X but was Y' and if you reverse them the message is confusing. For exceptions I use assertThrows which takes the exception class and a lambda — it also returns the exception so I can inspect the message. For testing multiple conditions I use assertAll, which runs all the assertions even if one fails, giving me a full picture of what's wrong rather than stopping at the first failure.

questions.question: What is a parameterized test in JUnit 5 and how do you write one?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Parameterized Tests | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **@ParameterizedTest** runs the same test with different inputs. Combined with `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource`, or `@MethodSource` to supply values. Avoids writing multiple identical tests for boundary conditions — a single method tests multiple cases.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know modern JUnit 5 features beyond just @Test
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing five identical test methods for five input values instead of one @ParameterizedTest
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show @CsvSource for multiple parameter sets and explain @MethodSource for complex object parameters

sections.title: Test Multiple Inputs with One Method
sections.content: `@ParameterizedTest` + `@ValueSource(ints = {1, 2, 3})` — test method receives one int. `@CsvSource({"1,2,3", "4,5,9"})` — multiple parameters per test case. `@MethodSource("provideArguments")` — static method returns `Stream<Arguments>` for complex objects. Requires `junit-jupiter-params` dependency. `@NullAndEmptySource` — automatically tests null and empty string cases.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @ParameterizedTest replaces @Test for parameterized cases
- @ValueSource: simple single-type values (ints, strings, booleans)
- @CsvSource: multiple params per row as comma-separated string
- @MethodSource: complex parameters via static Stream<Arguments>
- @EnumSource: iterate over enum values
- @NullAndEmptySource: adds null and empty to @ValueSource
- Requires: junit-jupiter-params dependency
- Each parameter set appears as separate test in report

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Parameterized tests let me run the same test logic with different inputs without duplicating code. I annotate the method with @ParameterizedTest and then specify the input source. For simple values I use @ValueSource — for example @ValueSource of ints with the values I want to test. For multiple parameters per test case, like input and expected output pairs, I use @CsvSource where each string is a CSV row. For complex objects I use @MethodSource pointing to a static method that returns a Stream of Arguments. Each parameter set shows up as its own test case in the test report, which is great for debugging which specific input failed.

questions.question: How do you test that a method throws an exception in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Test Exception JUnit 5 Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use `assertThrows(ExceptionClass.class, () -> methodCall())`**. It returns the thrown exception so you can verify the message. If the expected exception is NOT thrown, the test fails. This is the JUnit 5 way — JUnit 4 used `@Test(expected=Exception.class)`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of exception testing — a very common real-world test scenario
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using JUnit 4's @Test(expected=) syntax in JUnit 5, or using try-catch in tests instead of assertThrows
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show that assertThrows returns the exception for further inspection (message, cause) — more powerful than JUnit 4's approach

sections.title: assertThrows Returns the Exception
sections.content: `Exception ex = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> service.processAge(-1))`. The method under test must throw `IllegalArgumentException` — if it doesn't throw or throws a different type, test fails. The returned exception lets you chain: `assertEquals("Age cannot be negative", ex.getMessage())`. For asserting NO exception is thrown: `assertDoesNotThrow(() -> method())`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- assertThrows(ExceptionType.class, executable)
- Returns the thrown exception for further assertions
- Fails if: no exception thrown, or wrong exception type thrown
- Can then assert: ex.getMessage(), ex.getCause()
- assertDoesNotThrow: asserts method completes without exception
- JUnit 4 equivalent: @Test(expected = Exception.class) — less flexible
- Don't use try/catch in tests — it hides failures
- Executable: lambda () -> code or method reference

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In JUnit 5 I use assertThrows to test exception scenarios. I pass the expected exception class and a lambda containing the call that should throw. If the exception is thrown, assertThrows returns it — which is really useful because I can then assert on the message or cause. If no exception is thrown, or the wrong type is thrown, the test fails. I'd also note that I never use try-catch blocks in tests for exception verification — if you catch the exception yourself, a test that doesn't throw will silently pass when it should fail. The JUnit 5 approach is cleaner and more explicit than JUnit 4's @Test(expected) attribute.

questions.question: How is JUnit 5 different from JUnit 4? What are the main changes a fresher should know?
questions.title: JUnit 5 vs JUnit 4 Differences | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: JUnit 5 is modular (3 sub-projects), uses @ExtendWith instead of @RunWith, renamed annotations (@BeforeEach vs @Before, @Disabled vs @Ignore), has assertThrows and assertAll, and supports Java 8+ lambdas. It also dropped the public method requirement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the current framework and can explain why it changed — shows you're not just copying code blindly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using JUnit 4 annotations in a JUnit 5 project — @Before instead of @BeforeEach, @RunWith instead of @ExtendWith
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the modular architecture: JUnit Platform + Jupiter + Vintage — shows you understand the project structure

sections.title: Key Differences at a Glance
sections.content:
| JUnit 4 | JUnit 5 |
|---|---|
| @Before | @BeforeEach |
| @After | @AfterEach |
| @BeforeClass | @BeforeAll |
| @AfterClass | @AfterAll |
| @Ignore | @Disabled |
| @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner) | @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) |
| @Rule | @ExtendWith / no direct equivalent |
| Expected exception via @Test(expected=...) | assertThrows() |

JUnit 5 methods don't need to be public. JUnit 5 is three modules: Platform (launcher), Jupiter (new API), Vintage (runs JUnit 4 tests).

sections.title: Key Points
content: @Before → @BeforeEach | @After → @AfterEach
@BeforeClass → @BeforeAll | @AfterClass → @AfterAll
@Ignore → @Disabled | @RunWith → @ExtendWith
Methods no longer need to be public
assertThrows replaces @Test(expected=...)
assertAll for grouped assertions
JUnit 5 = Platform + Jupiter + Vintage
Vintage module: run JUnit 4 tests in JUnit 5 environment

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The main practical differences between JUnit 4 and 5 are annotation renames and a modular architecture. The lifecycle annotations were renamed to be more explicit: @Before became @BeforeEach, @BeforeClass became @BeforeAll, @Ignore became @Disabled. @RunWith was replaced with @ExtendWith for extensions like Mockito. For exceptions, @Test(expected=...) was replaced with assertThrows which is more powerful because you can inspect the exception. JUnit 5 also dropped the requirement that test methods be public. Architecturally, JUnit 5 is three modules: the Platform handles launching tests, Jupiter is the new programming model, and Vintage lets you still run old JUnit 4 tests. The reason this matters practically: if you see @RunWith in a project's test code, you're looking at JUnit 4 code, which means you need to be careful not to mix annotations.

questions.question: How do you add JUnit 5 to a Maven project?
questions.title: Add JUnit 5 to Maven Project | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Add the junit-jupiter dependency (or junit-bom for managed versions) and configure the maven-surefire-plugin 2.22.0+ which has native JUnit 5 support. The spring-boot-starter-test dependency includes JUnit 5 automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical setup knowledge — can you add testing to a project from scratch?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting maven-surefire-plugin configuration — tests compile but don't run without it on older Maven versions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention junit-bom (Bill of Materials) for version management, and that spring-boot-starter-test bundles JUnit 5 already

sections.title: Maven Configuration
sections.content:
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.10.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>3.0.0</version>
</plugin>
```
For Spring Boot projects: `spring-boot-starter-test` includes JUnit 5 + Mockito + AssertJ automatically — no extra dependency needed. Use `junit-bom` in `<dependencyManagement>` to align versions across JUnit 5 modules.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Dependency: org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:<version>:test
maven-surefire-plugin 2.22.0+ required for JUnit 5 support
spring-boot-starter-test: includes JUnit 5 + Mockito + AssertJ — use this for Spring projects
junit-bom: Bill of Materials for consistent JUnit module versions
Separate artifacts: junit-jupiter-api, junit-jupiter-engine, junit-jupiter-params
junit-jupiter aggregates all three for convenience
Run tests: mvn test — Surefire runs JUnit 5 tests automatically

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: For a plain Maven project, I add the junit-jupiter dependency with test scope and ensure the maven-surefire-plugin is at version 2.22 or later which has native JUnit 5 support. For Spring Boot projects, I don't need to do anything extra — spring-boot-starter-test already includes JUnit 5 along with Mockito and AssertJ. The most common mistake when setting up JUnit 5 in Maven is forgetting to configure the Surefire plugin — the tests will compile but not execute. I use mvn test to run tests from the command line.

questions.question: What is @Nested in JUnit 5 and when would you use it?
questions.title: @Nested JUnit 5 Tests | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @Nested allows test methods to be grouped inside inner classes, creating a hierarchical test structure. Use it to organize tests by scenario, feature, or state — e.g., a nested class for 'when user is logged in' vs 'when user is not logged in'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of test organization patterns — as projects grow, flat test classes become unreadable
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing every test in one flat class with long method names to express context — @Nested expresses context structurally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the 'given-context' pattern: each @Nested class describes a precondition or scenario, and inner @Test methods test the expectations in that context

sections.title: Hierarchical Test Organization
Key Points
content: @Nested: non-static inner class containing test methods
Each @Nested class can have its own @BeforeEach / @AfterEach
Parent @BeforeEach runs before child @BeforeEach — both execute
Use @DisplayName on @Nested for readable test reports
Common pattern: group tests by precondition/state
@Nested classes can be further nested
@BeforeAll in @Nested requires @TestInstance(PER_CLASS)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @Nested lets you create inner test classes inside your main test class to organize tests by scenario or state. Instead of a flat list of test methods with names like testGetUser_whenExists() and testGetUser_whenNotFound(), I can create two @Nested classes: one named 'when user exists' and one 'when user does not exist' — each with its own @BeforeEach setup and focused test methods. This creates a hierarchy in the test report that's much easier to read. Each @Nested class gets both the parent @BeforeEach and its own @BeforeEach executed, so I can share common setup in the parent and add scenario-specific setup in the nested class. I'd use this once a test class grows beyond maybe 15-20 tests and starts to feel disorganized.
